articles.body: The Valencia Port Authority has awarded the contract for the refurbishment of the steel structure of the elevated seafront promenade in the La Marina area of the Port of Valencia. The contract has been awarded to the joint venture SORIGUE ACSA CONSERVACIÓN DE INFRAESTRUCTURAS and ACSA OBRAS E INFRAESTRUCTURAS, with a budget of EUR 2,257,841 including VAT and an expected completion period of 15 months. The works encompass cleaning, repair and treatment of the steel structure to improve long-term preservation, repair of the benches and pergola located at the end of the promenade near the port entrance, and improvements to the safety and functionality of the pedestrian walkway including upgrades to access stairways, railings and lighting. The tender incorporates specific environmental conditions for the execution of works. To encourage the use of renewable energy, the use of electricity generators and compressors powered by combustion engines will be avoided, and materials suitable for reuse must be managed by an authorised waste management operator. The project forms part of a broader programme of port-city integration initiatives being undertaken or planned by the Port Authority in the Marina area, including improvements to the Customs Quay and the area surrounding the Clock Building, as well as the planned relocation of the former lighthouse.

articles.title: IMO DCS 2025: Is shipping’s decarbonisation progress fast enough?
articles.summary: Each year, the Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC) reviews a summary report that the IMO Secretariat prepares from verified data submitted by shipowners for the previous reporting year. The report covering 2025 data will be considered during the upcoming MEPC 85, scheduled for 30 November to 3 December...
articles.body: IMO DCS 2025: Is shipping’s decarbonisation progress fast enough? in International Shipping News 30/10/2026 Each year, the Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC) reviews a summary report that the IMO Secretariat prepares from verified data submitted by shipowners for the previous reporting year. The report covering 2025 data will be considered during the upcoming MEPC 85, scheduled for 30 November to 3 December 2026. The session will also be critical for discussions on the draft amendments incorporating the IMO Net-Zero Framework, ahead of the possible resumption of the extraordinary MEPC session on 4 December, when its adoption is due to be considered. Fuel consumption trends Annual fuel consumption was around 221 million tonnes in 2025, of which alternative fuels accounted for around 18.3 million tonnes. The use of alternative fuels[1] has been rising steadily, from 5.9% of the shipping energy demand[2] in 2019 to 9.5% in 2025. Source: IMO DCS, Drewry Maritime Research Biofuels maintained their strong momentum, with consumption doubling over the year. Their share of shipping’s alternative fuel demand increased to around 12% compared to 6.2% in 2024. The lead alternative fuel, LNG, has remained stable YoY in absolute consumption terms, with total LNG consumption remaining just short of 15 million tonnes. Methanol’s consumption has grown steadily, but its share among all alternative fuels remains stable at 0.3% on an energy basis. Ammonia is yet to make its debut in the IMO DCS reports, and the stakeholders anticipate seeing a new column for ammonia in next year’s data. Source: IMO DCS, Drewry Maritime Research Any impact on emissions? Despite continued growth in shipping activity, the industry reduced its overall CO₂ emissions by 1.3% in 2025. This came despite a 2% rise in vessel capacity and a 1% uptick in total distance sailed. Average emissions per vessel reduced 4%, while emissions per nautical mile contracted 2.3%. Increased biofuel consumption, which reached 2.5 million tonnes, and generally lower sailing speeds were among key drivers for this reduction. Source: IMO DCS, Drewry Maritime Research Despite the broader slowdown in fleet speeds, following the introduction of EEXI and CII, container ships and tankers recorded an increase in average speeds in 2025. This indicates robust demand and higher vessel utilisation, with longer sailing distances around the COGH, potentially contributing to the increase. Source: IMO DCS, Drewry Maritime Research In 2025, CO₂ emissions per vessel declined significantly, while CO₂ emissions per unit of distance (nautical mile) continued their gradual downward trend among vessels reporting to the IMO DCS. Source: IMO DCS, Drewry Maritime Research Shipping’s AER (supply-based carbon intensity[3]) also continued to improve in 2025, falling by a further 1.6% to reach 33.1% below 2008 levels. This aligns with the decline in CO₂ emissions during the year, despite growth in fleet capacity and distance sailed. If the shipping industry continues this reduction at the same rate, the IMO’s 40% carbon-intensity reduction target for 2030 seems achievable. Source: IMO DCS CII drives efficiency improvements With 2025 marking the third year of CII implementation, vessels were expected to strengthen their energy-efficiency measures to maintain or achieve compliance. This is reflected in a 4% increase in the share of compliant vessels[4] among those required to report CII ratings to the IMO DCS. At the same time, the share of vessels not reporting CII ratings declined from 8.9% to 3.6%. Combined with the improving AER trend discussed above, this indicates greater familiarity among ship operators with CII calculations and the measures needed to improve compliance. Note: Vessels that did not report their CII ratings are assumed to be non-compliant. Source: IMO DCS, Drewry Maritime Research Among the major cargo carrying sectors, a comparison of the 2025 CII data with the previous year’s ratings indicates that LNG carriers are struggling to maintain compliance under the regulation, with the sector’s share of compliant vessels declining 1.6% in 2025. LNG trade remains particularly exposed to geopolitical conflicts, which can alter trading patterns and consequently affect the sector’s GHG-emission performance. In 2025, shifting trade requirements increased demand for less-efficient LNG carriers, adding further pressure on the sector’s CII performance. Note: The above calculation includes vessels that did not reported their CII ratings to IMO DCS as non-compliant. Source: IMO DCS, Drewry Maritime Research Conclusion As the industry inches closer to the postponed MEPC ES2 (Extraordinary Session 2) planned for 4 December 2026 to further discuss the fate of the drafted ‘IMO Net Zero Framework’, Drewry’s analysis of the 2025 IMO DCS data shows some encouraging signs of progress. Despite vessel capacity improving 2% and distance sailed rising 1%, shipping managed to reduce its overall CO₂ emissions by 1.3% in 2025 (as compared to 2024). Shipping’s AER also improved further, taking supply-based carbon intensity to 33.1%, below 2008 levels, gradually closing the gap towards the IMO’s 40% reduction target for 2030. Alternative fuels continued to gain ground, accounting for around 9.5% of shipping’s energy demand in 2025. Biofuel blends remained the key growth story, with consumption more than doubling during the year to around 2.5 million tonnes. At the same time, the third year of CII implementation showed improving compliance, with the share of compliant vessels increasing by 4%. Overall, the 2025 numbers suggest shipping is moving in the right direction on efficiency and carbon intensity, but the pace remains gradual. With further consideration of the IMO’s mid-term measures expected at the resumed MEPC ES2 on 4 December 2026, an outcome with a price gap reduction mechanism could significantly impact the pace at which shipping moves from incremental efficiency improvements towards deeper emissions reductions. Source: Drewry 2026-10-30 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: How a New “Arab Dark Fleet” Keeps Hormuz Oil Flowing
articles.summary: Gulf oil producers have gained control of a fleet of nearly 230 tankers that have defied Iran to ship oil through the Strait of Hormuz and keep the chokepoint open to global trade. The giant fleet is owned, managed, chartered or controlled by Gulf national oil companies or their trading and shipping arms and is ...
articles.body: How a New “Arab Dark Fleet” Keeps Hormuz Oil Flowing in International Shipping News 30/10/2026 Gulf oil producers have gained control of a fleet of nearly 230 tankers that have defied Iran to ship oil through the Strait of Hormuz and keep the chokepoint open to global trade. The giant fleet is owned, managed, chartered or controlled by Gulf national oil companies or their trading and shipping arms and is designed to cut reliance on chartering tankers on the spot market. Despite very high freight rates, fewer shipowners will send tankers to load at oil terminals in Iraq, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain, Oman or the UAE. The result is a new fleet, the Arab Dark Fleet, solely deployed by Gulf states and dedicated to keeping their oil flowing. The “Arab Dark Fleet” is the biggest shift in how Gulf national oil companies run their freight, logistics, and supply chains since the Tanker War of the 1980s. Dark VLCC Shuttles Carry Oil to Ship-to-Ship Hubs Off the UAE and Oman The fleet almost exclusively sails dark in the Middle East Gulf, with AIS switched off for legitimate safety and security reasons. Tankers load dark, and then transit the Strait of Hormuz via Oman’s southern corridor with U.S. military support. Many have not signaled their AIS position in weeks. The majority of the fleet is very large crude carriers. This is the predominant class used to run shuttle trips from oil terminals west of Hormuz to ship-to-ship transfer hubs off the UAE and Oman. Ships sail with AIS switched off, often at night with oil, then transferred to other tankers for onward shipment to global markets. National Carriers and Global Traders Swell the Fleet The fleet includes tankers already owned by national shipping companies. These are supplemented by newly purchased tankers, chartered-in tonnage and spot charters, many of them from private Greek shipowners. Global traders are also shuttling oil that has been loaded at West-of-Hormuz terminals and then sold at a premium from ship-to-ship hubs or shipped directly to buyers. Their ships are included in the dark fleet tally. A South Korean Shipowner Becomes the Arab Dark Fleet’s Largest Operator The most important addition to the Arab Dark Fleet is a South Korean shipowner, half-owned by a large container line. The South Korean shipowner began buying and chartering VLCCs in December 2025 and has built a fleet of more than 100 ships, about 70% of which now work in the Arab Dark Fleet. Their tankers account for nearly 30% of the Arab Dark Fleet and make them the largest operator, followed by the national carriers. It is also the most targeted by Iran: Iran’s Persian Gulf Transit Authority has threatened legal action against their fleet for using the ‘unauthorized’ southern corridor. Gulf Producers Run the Tanker War Shuttle in Reverse For decades, shipping has run on the mantra that “cargo is king”. But Gulf producers have realized they must own or control tankers in order to move oil through the high-risk southern corridor in Omani waters, even if securing the supply chain equates to much higher freight costs. The same scenario was seen, in reverse, during the 1984–88 Tanker War. Owners refused to load at Iran’s Kharg Island even at high rates. Iran set up a VLCC shuttle from Kharg Island to the mouth of the Gulf, where cargoes were transferred to other tankers. Today the roles are reversed, with Arab producers running the shuttle under attack from Iran. Shuttling Oil Out of Hormuz Ties Up Global VLCC Capacity The rise of the Arab Dark Fleet has added to freight logistics inefficiencies and tied up some 15%-20% of the global VLCC fleet at any one time. Gulf oil companies are selling oil from ship-to-ship hubs at a discount to their official monthly selling price after shuttling it out of Hormuz. Shipbroker Braemar said on October 23 the freight cost of loading from Oman to Asia was around $15/bbl. What the Numbers Show About the Arab Dark Fleet • 80% are very large crude carriers, the dominant class in the fleet. 10% are aframaxes or LR2 tankers, the second-largest segment. • The average age is 12 years. • 28% are beneficially owned by the South Korean shipowner. • Gulf national oil companies beneficially own 36% of the fleet. • 40% are flagged in Liberia and 11% in the Marshall Islands, the two quality open registers run by U.S.-incorporated companies. Most of the Fleet Went Dark in the Past Three Months • 70% have had a dark period in the past three months, averaging 12 days. 10% had extended dark periods of more than four weeks. • Dark activity was concentrated in the Middle East Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea. The Fleet’s Expansion Lifts Hormuz Transits The expansion of the Arab Dark Fleet in recent months has been key to increased transits. Preliminary figures for crude exports (minus Iran) loaded at terminals West of Hormuz are running at a pace of about 11 million bpd over October, according to Vortexa data. That compares with 1.56 million bpd in May when Gulf states began using the southern corridor, and pre-war volumes of 14.5 million bpd. Gulf Shipowners Keep Buying Second-Hand Tankers Gulf shipowners continue buying second-hand tonnage for immediate use in the Arab Dark Fleet, focusing on VLCCs and Suezmaxes. In the past three months, one Gulf national shipping company spent nearly $2bn on vessels. Windward data show that some 15% of the Arab Dark Fleet has changed registered ownership in the past three months. Source: Windward 2026-10-30 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

Despite very high freight rates, fewer shipowners will send tankers to load at oil terminals in Iraq, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain, Oman or the UAE.
The result is a new fleet, the Arab Dark Fleet, solely deployed by Gulf states and dedicated to keeping their oil flowing.

articles.title: ZERO44 launches free calculator showing what switching to biofuel really costs
articles.summary: ZERO44, provider of software for maritime emissions compliance, has released a free, interactive fuel cost calculator on its website. articles.body: ZERO44 launches free calculator showing what switching to biofuel really costs in International Shipping News , Shipping: Emission Possible 30/10/2026 ZERO44, provider of software for maritime emissions compliance, has released a free, interactive fuel cost calculator on its website. The tool shows ship operators how the economics of replacing fossil fuel with biofuel change once carbon regulations are taken into account, and how that picture shifts year by year. Beyond the price per tonne According to ZERO44, fuel prices are still frequently compared on a one-to-one basis: what does a tonne of biofuel cost against a tonne of fossil fuel? If the comparison stops there, biofuel often loses due to its price premium. “Too often, the conversation about alternative fuels stops at the price per tonne,” says Friederike Hesse, Managing Director at ZERO44. “But that doesn’t tell the whole story. Once you factor in regulatory costs and the value of over-compliance, the premium can turn into a net benefit. We built this calculator to make those mechanics visible.” Fuel Cost Preview 2030 Under the calculator’s default assumptions, replacing one tonne of VLSFO with biodiesel on voyages within the EU results in a net benefit of around €163 in 2026. The outcome depends on many inputs: fossil and biofuel prices, the geographical scope of the voyage, and the prices for EU Allowances, FuelEU pooling and Scope 3 insets. The calculator brings these elements together in one view, allowing operators to understand the full picture. Regulatory costs are set to rise: EUA prices are expected to increase, FuelEU targets tighten every five years, and the IMO Net-Zero Framework could add a global carbon price from 2029 if adopted in December. The calculator shows users how these effects combine over the years. Fuel Cost 2026 A starting point, not a decision tool The calculator is intended for illustrative purposes only and is not part of the ZERO44 product. The company stresses that real fuel decisions are far more complex. Friederike Hesse: “Fleets operate on a diverse fuel mix, and some vessels are better candidates for alternative fuels than others, depending on engine compatibility and their trading patterns. On top of that, prices for fuels, allowances and surplus change continuously.” ZERO44’s compliance software handles this complexity. It offers similar but far more extensive analyses for a company’s own fleet, including forecasting and scenario planning across EU ETS, FuelEU Maritime, UK ETS, CII and carbon insetting. articles.body: MOL Signs Long-Term Charter Contract with Deutsche ReGas for Energie-Terminal “Deutsche Ostsee” in Germany in International Shipping News 30/10/2026 Mitsui O.S.K. Lines, Ltd. and Deutsche ReGas announced that they have entered into a long-term Time Charter Contract with Deutsche ReGas for the deployment of one FSRU at the Energie-Terminal “Deutsche Ostsee” in Mukran, Germany. Under this long-term arrangement, the LNG carrier will be converted at Hudong-Zhonghua Shipbuilding (Group) Co., Ltd.(“HZ”) in China and Deutsche ReGas will charter the FSRU from MOL starting in 2028. While MOL has previously undertaken FSRU conversion projects in collaboration with partner companies for their specific use, the Project marks FSRU conversion project on MOL’s sole initiative to be developed for LNG deliveries to major gas networks. The commemorative ceremony was held in Tokyo on October 29th, with relevant parties in attendance, including Deutsche ReGas CEO Ingo Wagner and MOL President & CEO Jotaro Tamura. Leveraging the expertise and know-how cultivated through our extensive LNG transportation track record with the world’s largest LNG carrier fleet, MOL has been expanding vertically into the downstream segment of the LNG value chain, including LNG receiving and regasification. Through the Project, MOL will provide a reliable and flexible LNG import solution for the German and European gas markets, thereby promoting the diversification of gas supply sources and the expansion of LNG import capacity, and contributing to a stable energy supply across Europe. At the commemorative ceremony in Tokyo (From left: Deutsche ReGas Marcus CCO, Deutsche ReGas Ingo CEO, MOL Tamura CEO, MOL Inomoto MEO, MOL Suryan MEO) Mr. Jotaro Tamura, President & CEO of MOL, commented: “The FSRU Project represents a major strategic milestone for MOL. We are pleased to partner with Deutsche ReGas on this important infrastructure Project and to work together with HZ to deliver an FSRU solution. Through this FSRU Project, MOL will further strengthen its position as a global provider of LNG infrastructure while contributing to Germany’s and Europe’s import solution.” Mr Suryan Wirya-Simunovic, Managing Executive Officer, commented: “The FSRU Project is a landmark achievement for MOL Europe and Africa Region and reflects our commitment to developing critical energy infrastructure that supports Europe’s evolving energy needs. By combining MOL’s global LNG expertise with Deutsche ReGas’s strong market position and leading operatorship in Germany, we are creating a reliable and flexible solution that will contribute to supply security and energy resilience in the region. We look forward to working closely with all Project partners to ensure the successful delivery and long-term operation of the terminal.” Ingo Wagner, Chief Executive Officer of Deutsche ReGas, commented: “We are excited about the future partnership with MOL as the leading player in floating LNG infrastructure. As the only LNG-Terminal in the eastern part of Germany and critical infrastructure, Deutsche ReGas has demonstrated its strategic importance for security of supply. By restoring the Terminal’s fully permitted capacity, we are continuing the path which we started in 2024. This allows to strengthen long-term energy security and creates additional import flexibility benefiting consumers, industry and energy markets alike. Formidable energy companies are reliable partners for us an infrastructure provider.” Image of LNG value chain (FSRU is positioned in the downstream segment) In BLUE ACTION 2035 Phase 2, the MOL Group has positioned portfolio strategy as one of its core strategies, with FSRU business serving as a stable earnings-generating business in the downstream segment of the LNG value chain. Through this Project, MOL aims to contribute to the stable supply of energy in Germany and Europe while further strengthening its energy infrastructure business. Source: Mitsui O.S.K. articles.body: GeoMarineHub Lets Ship Crews Email A Requisition As It Is, And Gives Verified Suppliers A Public Badge in International Shipping News 30/10/2026 GeoMarineHub, the Dubai-based ship-supply marketplace, today opened two changes to how vessels buy stores and how buyers check suppliers. Email the requisition as it is. Masters, chief engineers and purchasing officers can now forward a requisition to [email protected] in the form it already has: an Excel sheet, a Word table, a PDF or a scanned list. The platform reads every line, matches it to its IMPA code where one exists, and sends back a receipt that lists what it read: the vessel, the port, the ETA and each line. Nobody has to retype anything or open an account. Once the buyer confirms the receipt, the request goes to the verified suppliers at that port, who bid sealed, line by line. A public “Verified on GeoMarineHub” badge. Every supplier on the platform passes a company check before it can bid: the trade licence, the ownership, and the bank details the platform pays to. Verified suppliers now have a public verification page, and a badge they can place on their website, email signature and quotations. A buyer who has never dealt with a chandler can see in one click that the company’s documents were checked, which ports it serves, and what it supplies. The badge stays live only while the verification is current. “A vessel’s crew sends a list of 100 or more items to a few chandlers they already know, then compares PDFs by hand while the ship is two days out,” said Sherif Awad, founder of GeoMarineHub, whose family has supplied ships since 1981. “We wanted to take the friction out of both ends: the buyer sends the list exactly as it is, and the supplier he has never met can show it has been checked.” GeoMarineHub is free for buyers, with no commission on purchases. The platform has 60 verified suppliers at 49 ports in 19 countries and a catalogue of more than 50,000 IMPA-coded items. It covers ship supply, bunkering and fresh water, port agency, freight and chartering. GeoMarineHub is a marketplace only: it does not buy or resell goods itself. articles.body: IMO launches Blue Solutions to support maritime decarbonization in Southeast Asia in International Shipping News 30/10/2026 IMO has launched Blue Solutions, a new project intended to support maritime decarbonization in Southeast Asia. The announcement was made at the 51st ASEAN Maritime Transport Working Group (MTWG) Meeting in Phnom Penh, Cambodia. IMO will implement the project in collaboration with Partnerships in Environmental Management for the Seas of East Asia (PEMSEA) and six partner countries: Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Thailand and Viet Nam. A key feature of the project is its focus on ports, and their potential role in maritime decarbonization, helping countries assess and demonstrate solutions such as port and vessel electrification, cleaner technologies and operational improvements. The project will also support the development of greenhouse gas emission baselines and national action plans, and strengthen capacity-building, partnerships and knowledge-sharing across the region. The project is funded by the International Climate Initiative (IKI) of the Government of Germany, with an initially approved budget of EUR 5.9 million for Phase 1, and is expected to run until January 2031. The International Climate Initiative (IKI) said: “The transition to low-carbon shipping presents an important opportunity for Southeast Asia to strengthen its maritime competitiveness while contributing to global climate goals. Through Blue Solutions, we are pleased to support practical, country-driven action that can demonstrate scalable solutions and deliver tangible environmental and economic benefits across the region.” Welcoming the initiative, Aimee Gonzales, Executive Director of PEMSEA highlighted the importance of linking ports with wider transport and coastal development strategies: “Ports are critical nodes connecting maritime transport, energy systems, industry and surrounding communities. By combining IMO’s expertise in maritime decarbonization with PEMSEA’s experience in integrated coastal management, including green port development, Blue Solutions provides an opportunity to support practical, locally driven solutions that deliver benefits both within ports and across the wider transport system.” The project aims to support ports in moving from ambition to implementation, and to help create conditions for innovation, investment and the deployment of practical low-emission solutions across Southeast Asia. Welcoming the launch of Blue Solutions, Jose Matheickal, Director of IMO’s Technical Cooperation and Implementation Division, said: “Maritime decarbonization requires strong partnerships. Through Blue Solutions, we are bringing together governments, ports, industry and development partners to identify practical solutions, build local capacity and create pathways for implementation. By working together, we can accelerate the transition to a more sustainable maritime future.” Blue Solutions will be implemented under IMO’s wider GreenVoyage2050 Programme, drawing on its technical expertise, partnerships and knowledge-sharing networks while complementing ongoing efforts to accelerate maritime decarbonization in developing countries. Source: IMO 2026-10-30 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: Research Council will fund Norwegian maritime nuclear energy and propulsion project
articles.summary: The Marine Nuclear Propulsion System (MarNuPS) Pilot project has secured NOK 20 million (USD 2m) in initial funding from the Research Council of Norway as partners prepare to move maritime nuclear propulsion from system development towards physical integration and testing. Led by Emerald Nuclear Norway, MarNuPS...
articles.body: Research Council will fund Norwegian maritime nuclear energy and propulsion project in International Shipping News , Shipping: Emission Possible 30/10/2026 The Marine Nuclear Propulsion System (MarNuPS) Pilot project has secured NOK 20 million (USD 2m) in initial funding from the Research Council of Norway as partners prepare to move maritime nuclear propulsion from system development towards physical integration and testing. Led by Emerald Nuclear Norway, MarNuPS brings together VARD Group, Vard Electro, Island Offshore, NTNU, Imperial College London and Maskindynamikk in a consortium spanning reactor technology, ship design and integration, vessel operations, automation and academic research. The Research Council support comes in addition to substantial self-financing by the project partners. Stage 1 of the programme alone has an estimated total cost of around NOK 150m (USD 15.6m). “This award is evidence of validation and momentum rather than the scale of the ambition,” said Hallgeir Juliebø, Co-Founder and Chief Commercial Officer of Emerald Nuclear and Chairman of Emerald Nuclear Norway. “The partners are already making a substantial commitment to MarNuPS, and this support gives the programme additional backing as we move from design and analysis towards building and testing a complete integrated system. It’s only the beginning of a longer development and qualification process, but it demonstrates that maritime nuclear propulsion is now being pursued as a serious industrial project.” The MarNuPS Pilot will integrate Emerald Nuclear’s 5 MWe Gem Microreactor technology with energy storage, power conversion, vessel power management, automation and bridge control systems. Stage 1, planned for 2027, will establish an integrated test facility at Stette outside Ålesund. A full-scale representation of the shipboard propulsion system will be assembled and tested using electric heating instead of nuclear fuel, allowing the partners to study how the different systems perform together under conditions representative of vessel operations. Testing will cover normal operation, rapid changes in power demand, transient and stress conditions, system performance and crew interaction. Island Offshore plans to be the first shipowner to install the reactor and energy system, with vessel deployment targeted for 2031/32. “Nuclear energy has the potential to provide a new route to decarbonising offshore vessels without compromising the power, endurance and operational flexibility these ships require,” said Tommy Walaunet, CEO of Island Offshore. “Our role is to ensure that the system is developed around real offshore operations and the people who will ultimately use it. Our ambition is to be the first shipowner to install the system and demonstrate its potential in practice.” The partners bring complementary expertise: Emerald Nuclear in reactor technology and nuclear integration; VARD Group in ship design and integration; Vard Electro in power management and automation; Island Offshore in vessel operations and crew input; NTNU in nuclear and thermo-hydraulic modelling; Imperial College London in structural integrity; and Maskindynamikk in instrumentation, diagnostics and condition monitoring. Hallgeir Juliebø, Co-Founder and Chief Commercial Officer of Emerald Nuclear and Chairman of Emerald Nuclear Norway (Photo: Emerald Nuclear Norway) MarNuPS builds on several years of Norwegian research into maritime nuclear propulsion, including the NTNU-led NuProShip programme, in which Emerald Nuclear is also a partner. It is also an important element in the demonstration project tied to SFI SAINT – Sustainable, Applied and Industrialized Nuclear Technology, the national research centre that has received NOK 96 million from the Research Council alongside around NOK 200 million in industry contributions. Emerald Nuclear is a Tier 1 SAINT member. Together, these programmes are moving Norway’s maritime nuclear effort from research and feasibility towards industrialisation, testing and eventual vessel deployment. articles.title: Bangladesh: Shipbuilding industry awaits govt impetus for export boost
articles.summary: A government plan is afoot to nudge shipbuilding industry through up-scaling design capabilities, upgrading infrastructure and ensuring compliance with international standards so entrepreneurs can tap into European and North American markets. Commerce Ministry officials have elaborated on the move meant for enabling...
articles.body: Bangladesh: Shipbuilding industry awaits govt impetus for export boost in Shipbuilding News 30/10/2026 A government plan is afoot to nudge shipbuilding industry through up-scaling design capabilities, upgrading infrastructure and ensuring compliance with international standards so entrepreneurs can tap into European and North American markets. Commerce Ministry officials have elaborated on the move meant for enabling the non-traditional export industry to substantially supplement Bangladesh’s export earnings. Although a Tk 20-billion refinancing fund has been set up for the sector, shipyard owners say they have been unable to draw on it because of stringent eligibility conditions. Bangladesh Bank issued on February 8 a circular extending the refinancing scheme, which aims to promote the development and growth of the seaside shipbuilding industry. Under the scheme, participating banks were initially allowed to apply for refinancing until June 30, 2024, according to the circular. Considering the industry’s potential to boost export earnings, the central bank has extended the deadline for participating banks to seek refinancing against loans or investments extended to customers under the scheme to December 31, 2026, the circular said. Entrepreneurs have urged the ministry to get the circular revised and the conditions eased, ministry officials have said. Entrepreneurs also say lack of bank guarantees and high borrowing costs are keeping local shipyards from securing large export orders, with some contracts going to competitors such as India and Vietnam. Bangladesh economic report Talking to The Financial Express, Engr Abdur Rashid, managing director of Karnaphuli Dry Dock, said building a ship could take up to two and a half years, which makes high borrowing costs a major challenge for local shipbuilders. Given such long production cycles, shipyards need affordable financing and adequate guarantees to compete for international orders, he said. “We have had a refinancing fund for the sector for the past five years, but no one has been able to access financing from it,” he said, urging the government to relax the eligibility conditions. Without bank guarantees, he said, international buyers were placing large orders with shipyards in countries such as India and Vietnam. Referring to India, Mr Rashid said the country spends billions of dollars on foreign shipping companies and has framed a shipbuilding policy to build domestic capacity and keep more of that spending at home. “Bangladesh should likewise introduce more accessible financing arrangements so that local shipyards can capitalise on growing global opportunities.” Rising labour costs are making shipbuilding less attractive in some European and North American countries, opening room for Bangladesh to expand its presence on the global market, he noted. “However, we are failing to seize this opportunity because of inadequate policy support,” he added. Welcoming the new government’s interest in the sector, he said stronger policy support could draw large conglomerates into shipbuilding, a capital-intensive industry, and help Bangladesh secure a stronger position globally. At an event in Chattogram about two weeks ago, Commerce Minister Khandaker Abdul Muktadir said the government was prioritising policy and infrastructure support for the shipbuilding sector to tap global market opportunities and boost ship exports. He said coordinated public-private efforts were under way to strengthen domestic capacity and address the difficulties private shipyards face in obtaining bank guarantees. The government was also considering setting up a modern design-and skills-development centre in partnership with countries such as Norway and the Netherlands to help local shipbuilders meet international standards, he added. Identifying bank guarantees as a major obstacle to executing export orders, the minister said a hybrid model involving private companies and Bangladesh Navy-run dockyards was being worked out. Under the proposed arrangement, private companies would be able to execute shipbuilding orders by accessing bank-guarantee facilities under government supervision. He also said a high-level committee comprising representatives of the shipping, commerce, and environment, forest and climate change ministries would work to develop the shipbuilding and ship-recycling industries. Ministry officials stressed the need for modern cranes, fabrication facilities, design infrastructure and additional construction docks to realise Chattogram Dry Dock’s potential for building large vessels. Bangladesh exported ships, boats and floating structures worth $22.53 million in the fiscal year (FY) 2025-26, according to Export Promotion Bureau (EPB) data. articles.body: Port of Santos starts ethanol bunkering for ships in Port News 30/10/2026 The operation marks the transition from a trial to a regular ethanol supply model, the Santos port authority said. The first operation took place on 19 October, when the 13,000 TEU container ship CMA CGM IRON was refuelled at the Port of Santos. The vessel has an Everllence tri-fuel engine, which the partners said is the world’s first certified to operate on ethanol. This follows the pilot operation carried out in July, through a partnership between CMA CGM, Copersucar, Bunker One, AGEO Terminais, Santos Brasil and the Santos Port Authority (APS). “Following the first operation carried out in July, we are now moving into a new phase, demonstrating that ethanol can be incorporated into maritime operations safely, reliably and on a commercial scale,” said Giovani Grassi, CEO of CMA CGM Brazil. Ethanol produced by mills associated with Copersucar is supplied and transported to the Port of Santos by Evolua Etanol, Copersucar’s ethanol trading arm. It is stored at the port by AGEO Terminais, a liquid bulk storage operator. For the refuelling phase, which takes place at the Santos Brasil terminal, Bunker One created a protocol taking into account the low flash point of the fuel. The company claims the protocol is a first of its kind in Latin America. Citing figures from classification society DNV, the port authority said 159 ships already operate with methanol-capable engines that can also take ethanol, and more than 450 newbuilds with the same technology are due for delivery by 2030. articles.body: Kalmar updates its strategy and sets new performance targets for 2030 including a renewed framework for the capital allocation in Port News 30/10/2026 The Board of Directors of Kalmar Corporation has approved an updated strategy and performance targets for the strategy period until 2030. The updated strategy shifts Kalmar’s focus towards accelerated growth and lifetime value and strengthens the company’s position as a forerunner in intelligent and sustainable heavy material handling solutions. Kalmar’s strategic focus areas until 2030 are 1) Investing in sustainable innovations, 2) Accelerating services and customer lifetime value and 3) Driving growth. Kalmar’s key performance targets by 2030 are: • Sales growth exceeding 8% per annum over the cycle (previous target: 5%) • Comparable operating profit margin of 16% by 2030 (previous target: 15% by 2028) • Return on capital employed (ROCE) exceeding 25% by 2030 (unchanged) • Eco portfolio accounting for more than 50% of sales by 2030 (new target) • Services sales of EUR 800 million by 2030 (new target) • Additional gross efficiency improvements of EUR 50 million by the end of 2030 (new target) In addition to key performance targets, Kalmar remains committed to the near and long-term science-based emissions reduction targets with the Science Based Targets Initiative (SBTi). Kalmar aims for a dividend payout ratio of 30–50% (unchanged). The leverage target is to have a net debt to EBITDA ratio below 2.5x (previously <2.0x). As part of its capital allocation framework, Kalmar aims to pursue targeted acquisitions that support its strategy and complement organic growth. Kalmar’s guidance for 2026 remains unchanged: Kalmar expects its comparable operating profit margin to be above 12.5 percent in 2026. “Over the past two years, we’ve built a strong foundation as an independent and more service focused company. Now, we are accelerating our sustainable and profitable growth with an even stronger focus on customer lifetime value. By delivering intelligent, autonomous, and data-driven sustainable solutions alongside expanded services, we empower our customers to thrive while delivering high value to our shareholders,” says Sami Niiranen, President and CEO of Kalmar. President and CEO Sami Niiranen and other members of Kalmar’s leadership team will present the company’s updated strategy and performance targets in detail at Kalmar’s Capital Markets Day on November 2, 2026. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Noble Intrepid jack-up rig Source: Noble Corporation U.S.-headquartered offshore drilling contractor Noble Corporation is fueling its fleet utilization uptick with multimillion-dollar drilling assignments off the coasts of Uruguay, Nigeria, Ghana, Peru, and Norway, enabling its total contract backlog to hit $6.7 billion in the third quarter of 2026. articles.body: Fugro Arms Survey Fleet Against GPS Jamming After $28M Earnings Hit Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 30, 2026 Illustration (Credit: Fugro) Dutch geological data specialist Fugro said on Friday that Iran war-linked disruptions had dented its earnings by €25 million ($28 million) this year, including €10 million in the third quarter alone, while GPS jamming and restrictions on vessel movements continued to hamper Gulf offshore operations. Some clients in the region have altered project plans and, in some cases, used their own vessels for work that would otherwise have been contracted to Fugro, CEO Mark Heine told Reuters. "We have work, but it's not always possible to work because you have no navigation because the signals are being blocked, jammed," Heine said, adding that GPS interference could prevent survey vessels from carrying out work safely and accurately. To mitigate the operational impact, Fugro has begun deploying new antennas and software designed to filter out or block jamming signals, allowing vessels to continue operating in affected areas. Heine said some of the technology was already commercially available, while the company was also testing more advanced systems to further improve its resilience against interference. The equipment has already been installed on several vessels and will be rolled out across Fugro's fleet operating in exposed areas. "That makes a difference already," Heine said. Fugro also provides satellite positioning services through its Starfix technology, which is used to improve the accuracy and reliability of GPS signals. The investment will deepen, widen and improve the alignment of key harbour channels to strengthen marine access and improve operational efficiency and reliability across the gateway. The announcement builds on a sustained transformation of Port Saint John through the West Side Modernisation Project, which expanded berth, container handling and rail capabilities to bring annual on-dock container capacity above 800,000 TEUs. Private-sector partners have also invested more than CA$ 750 million in equipment and rail upgrades over the past decade, strengthening Saint John’s position as a Canadian trade gateway with modern terminals, greater capacity and stronger transportation connections. The channel improvements are designed to make the existing infrastructure work more effectively together, improving marine access for vessels and enhancing the overall resilience of the gateway and its transportation networks. The investment aligns with Canada’s ambition to double exports to non-US markets, with Port Saint John positioned to make a meaningful contribution by providing businesses with a dependable gateway and transportation options as they pursue new international customers.

articles.body: Interconnectors October 30, 2026 · 3 hours ago €3.1 billion Spain-France interconnector is 70% complete NS Nadja Skopljak Managing Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Red Eléctrica The multibillion-euro Biscay Gulf interconnector, set to increase electricity exchange capacity between Spain and France from 2.8 GW to 5 GW, is 70% complete, with onshore cable laying currently underway. Spanish transmission system operator (TSO) Red Eléctrica has begun underground cable laying for the electrical interconnection project that will, across the Bay of Biscay, connect Gatika in Spain and France's Cubnezais. Work will continue on the sections off the coast of Gipuzkoa between November and February, with all sections expected to be laid in French waters until the summer. The Spanish TSO also reported that the construction of the future Gatika converter station is progressing well, with civil engineering work completed and the electromechanical assembly currently underway. The Biscay Gulf interconnector is now 70% complete. Developed by Red Eléctrica and its French counterpart RTE, through the joint venture Inelfe, the project is considered a Project of Common Interest by the European Union and is co-financed through CINEA - the European Union's Climate, Infrastructure and Environment Executive Agency, in addition to support from the European Investment Bank (EIB). articles.body: Ports and Logistics Dockworkers unite across 113 ports in global anti-war protest Sam Chambers October 30, 2026 0 619 1 minute read CGT CGT One of the largest coordinated port labour mobilisations in history is underway today, with more than 25 unions staging strikes and demonstrations at 113 ports across 22 countries and territories. The worldwide action, organised under the banner “Dockworkers do not work for war”, has expanded dramatically from a smaller mobilisation involving 20 ports across seven countries in February. Major gateways involved include Hamburg, Le Havre, Marseille, Genoa, Gioia Tauro, Piraeus, Tangier Med, Mersin and India’s Nhava Sheva. France’s CGT has called a 24-hour walkout across approximately 24 ports, predicting that as much as 95% of national port activity could be halted. Italy has registered a nationwide 24-hour ports strike, coinciding with a general strike affecting other transport sectors. In Greece, seafarers’ unions have called 24-hour stoppages expected to disrupt ferry services at Piraeus, Rafina, Lavrio, Patras and Igoumenitsa. Organisers estimate that participating unions represent workers handling around 40% of Mediterranean container traffic, with up to 40,000 containers potentially delayed.< However, the actual disruption remains uncertain. Some ports are holding demonstrations rather than stopping cargo operations, while Genoa’s port authority anticipates relatively limited disruption. The campaign primarily opposes military cargo shipments through civilian ports, alongside demands for improved wages, working conditions and protections against automation. Although unprecedented in scale for this particular campaign, claims that it is the world’s largest port strike remain unverified. An international solidarity campaign for Liverpool dockworkers in January 1997 involved 105 ports and cities across 27 countries. No further worldwide coordinated strike date has been announced. Separately, a potential November 1 strike involving 250 port watchmen threatens operations at Los Angeles and Long Beach, although negotiations to avert the stoppage are continuing. Italy also faces another national general strike on November 20. articles.title: Oil majors count the cost of runaway tanker rates
articles.summary: Soaring tanker freight rates are taking an increasingly heavy toll on the world’s oil majors, with the latest quarterly results revealing billions of dollars in additional shipping-related liabilities, squeezed refining margins and losses on trading positions. Shell has disclosed a $5.4bn non-cash increase in its...
articles.body: Europe Tankers Oil majors count the cost of runaway tanker rates Sam Chambers October 30, 2026 0 473 2 minutes read Shell Shell Soaring tanker freight rates are taking an increasingly heavy toll on the world’s oil majors, with the latest quarterly results revealing billions of dollars in additional shipping-related liabilities, squeezed refining margins and losses on trading positions. Shell has disclosed a $5.4bn non-cash increase in its shipping lease liabilities during the third quarter, reflecting the extraordinary rise in tanker rates since the outbreak of the Middle East conflict. The accounting adjustment relates to index-linked vessel charters, which must be revalued using prevailing spot rates. Shell’s shipping lease liabilities have increased by nearly $7.7bn since the beginning of the year, although the company stressed that the revaluations do not represent immediate cash expenditure. Oil majors: VLCC earnings this month were 14 times their ten-year average Shell chief financial officer Sinead Gorman said freight rates between the Middle East and China were now around ten times their levels a year ago. “You see that starting to come into margins,” she told analysts, adding that higher transportation costs were affecting refining, chemicals and crude trading. The British major nevertheless reported adjusted third-quarter earnings of $10.8bn, more than double the year-earlier figure, benefiting from exceptionally strong refining margins. At TotalEnergies, chief executive Patrick Pouyanné revealed that shipping costs, previously around $2 to $3 per barrel, had climbed to approximately $25 per barrel. Pouyanné attributed around $6 per barrel of pressure on the company’s liquids price realisations to additional freight costs. The French major has some protection through its chartering strategy, with fixed-rate medium- and long-term agreements covering approximately 40% of the equity crude it lifts. Pouyanné said having tankers available at agreed rates had also allowed the company’s traders to profit from moving Iraqi crude through the Strait of Hormuz. Italian energy giant Eni has similarly acknowledged that rising shipping costs are eating into its refining earnings The company reported third-quarter refining adjusted operating profit of €730m, supported by strong margins and increased refinery utilisation, but said the gains were partly offset by higher freight costs and unfavourable crude differentials. Eni executive Pino Ricci confirmed that the company’s refining margin calculations incorporated the sharp increase in transportation costs resulting from the Hormuz crisis. Norway’s Equinor has reported a more direct trading impact. Its crude, products and liquids business swung to an adjusted operating loss of $96m in the third quarter, compared with a $355m profit in the preceding three months. Equinor attributed the deterioration to losses on derivative positions in the exceptionally tight shipping market, which more than offset strong products trading. The Norwegian major also identified increased freight rates as an important contributor to higher operating expenses during the first nine months of 2026. Oil majors hoping for some freight rate reprieve would have been disappointed with the bullish mood at this week’s Maritime CEO Forum in Monaco where tanker owners appeared in no hurry to call the top of the market. Arrow researcher Burak Cetinok calculated that VLCC earnings this month were 14 times their ten-year average, with the weekly multiple approaching 20, but saw no immediate sell signal. DHT Holdings chief executive Svein Moxnes Harfjeld argued that fleet ageing would help underpin the market. By the end of 2029, almost half the VLCC fleet will be over 15 years old and a quarter over 20, creating substantial replacement requirements. Alberta Shipmanagement’s Alexia Inglessis pointed to recovering Middle Eastern oil flows, stronger Chinese demand, depleted inventories and sanctions-related inefficiencies. “I think we have a lot of things that point to a good market for the short to medium term,” she said. articles.title: Maritime CEO Forum: When to leave the party
articles.summary: Shipping investors are enjoying extraordinary returns but face increasingly difficult decisions over when to cash out, with industry leaders warning that geopolitical disruption is masking underlying market risks and encouraging potentially dangerous investment decisions. Speaking at the Money and Ships session of...
articles.body: Europe Finance and Insurance Maritime CEO Maritime CEO Forum: When to leave the party Splash October 30, 2026 0 341 2 minutes read Splash Splash Shipping investors are enjoying extraordinary returns but face increasingly difficult decisions over when to cash out, with industry leaders warning that geopolitical disruption is masking underlying market risks and encouraging potentially dangerous investment decisions. Speaking at the Money and Ships session of this week’s Maritime CEO Forum at the Yacht Club de Monaco, Christoph Toepfer, chief executive of Borealis Maritime, warned that shipping was “living on borrowed time” as conflicts and trade disruptions continue to inflate tonne-mile demand. “I always enjoy staying late at the party,” Toepfer said, before suggesting that the resolution of geopolitical crises could rapidly unwind some of the demand supporting today’s markets. Andy Dacy, CEO and CIO of JP Morgan Asset Management’s Global Transportation Group, was more optimistic, suggesting shipping had another 12 to 18 months of strong earnings ahead. “We’re on a plateau of some sort for at least the foreseeable future,” he said. Dacy pointed to the enormous number of vessels delivered between 2004 and 2012 that will approach recycling age over the coming years, providing a potential counterweight to any reduction in geopolitical disruption. “We have at least another 12 to 18 months of good times ahead of us based on bad things, of course,” he observed. CTM chief executive Carlos Pena was less convinced about current tanker valuations, suggesting owners should consider selling VLCCs at today’s elevated prices while remaining invested in dry bulk, which has yet to enjoy comparable earnings. The discussion, moderated by TURTLE chief executive Isabelle Rickmers, also revealed sharply contrasting definitions of successful investment. Toepfer recalled turning a $10m investment in a containership into $37m before reinvesting the proceeds in two large anchor handlers, subsequently sold for $130m. Pena argued that sometimes the best investment decision was accepting substantial losses early. Closing expensive charter positions had allowed CTM to survive and develop its pool operations. “You need to have courage and lose money,” Pena said. Massimo Giovannini, managing partner of TST Group, agreed, recalling his decision not to buy six Korean-built handysizes at approximately $17m apiece in 2014, ahead of years of depressed dry bulk earnings. Despite expectations of another downturn, the panellists were divided over whether shipping would experience another genuine financial crisis. Toepfer argued that strong balance sheets, abundant cash and low leverage would prevent widespread distress, with investors ready to acquire vessels whenever prices weakened. “I don’t think we will see a proper distressed market in the next 10 years,” he said, suggesting listed shipping companies might offer greater discounts than privately owned vessels during the next downturn. Dacy was more cautious, predicting a downturn within five years while highlighting how shipping’s reduced borrowing requirements had insulated it from intensifying competition for capital. “AI is sucking up capital across the board,” he warned, although shipowners currently have sufficient cash to repay debt rather than seek additional financing. Pena stressed that financing remained available for attractive projects but advised newcomers to shipping to gain experience before committing capital at today’s prices. The panellists also identified protectionism, a possible Taiwan crisis and speculative newbuilding orders as major threats, particularly unfixed containerships and car carriers scheduled for delivery several years from now. Technology, supposedly the answer to many of shipping’s problems, came under scrutiny in two thought-provoking Splash contributions this week. articles.title: San Pedro Bay identifies LNG and methanol as near-term priorities
articles.summary: The ports of Long Beach and Los Angeles have released a comprehensive Clean Marine Fuel Feasibility Assessment identifying the most promising alternative marine fuels for oceangoing vessels calling at the nation’s busiest port complex, conducted as part of their joint Green Shipping Corridor efforts. The study...
articles.body: The ports of Long Beach and Los Angeles have released a comprehensive Clean Marine Fuel Feasibility Assessment identifying the most promising alternative marine fuels for oceangoing vessels calling at the nation’s busiest port complex, conducted as part of their joint Green Shipping Corridor efforts. The study examined which fuels are most likely to be adopted by the shipping industry, how much demand could develop locally and what infrastructure would be required to support their adoption. The assessment found that liquefied natural gas and methanol are the two most viable clean marine fuels for the near and medium term. With approximately 4,000 vessels calling at San Pedro Bay ports annually, oceangoing ships represent the largest single source of emissions in the complex and are central to Clean Air Action Plan goals. By 2030, annual demand at the two ports could reach approximately 65,000 to 115,000 metric tonnes of LNG and 64,000 to 250,000 metric tonnes of methanol, depending on market conditions and vessel deployment. The study found that much of the storage and distribution infrastructure needed for early methanol fuelling is already available or adaptable, reducing the need for major initial investment. For LNG, the assessment recommends focusing on existing ship-to-ship fuelling methods rather than constructing major new storage facilities. The study also found that shipping lines are investing in a variety of fuel technologies rather than converging on a single alternative to conventional marine fuel, with fuel costs, shipping line commitments and regulatory requirements the key determinants of adoption pace. The assessment recommends a phased approach encompassing incentives for early methanol use, pilot fuelling projects, utilisation of existing storage facilities and collaboration with regulatory agencies on safety and permitting requirements. The findings will inform a joint Request for Proposal anticipated by the end of the year seeking proposals to demonstrate alternative fuel bunkering capabilities in San Pedro Bay, and will guide future planning with shipping lines, fuel suppliers, terminal operators and government agencies.

articles.body: Middle East Tankers Tanker targeted with hull-mounted explosives in Hormuz Sam Chambers October 30, 2026 0 417 1 minute read IMO IMO A tanker has been set ablaze in the Strait of Hormuz after attackers aboard a small boat attached explosives directly to its hull, marking a worrying new tactic in the campaign against commercial shipping. The Panama-flagged, 159,092 dwt Louise 1 was attacked late yesterday, 25 nautical miles northeast of Khasab, Oman, according to maritime security firm Vanguard Tech. UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported that a small boat approached the tanker’s port side and attached two explosive devices above the waterline. The resulting explosions sparked an engine room fire and temporarily disabled the vessel. The blaze has since been extinguished and the tanker has resumed its voyage. All crew are safe and no pollution has been reported. The attack represents a departure from the missile, drone and small-arms strikes that have dominated Iranian attacks on merchant shipping during the eight-month conflict. Meanwhile, a separate maritime security incident initially reported as involving a burning tanker has been clarified by UKMTO as a regional trading dhow. The vessel caught fire, listed and sank, with its crew safely evacuated. Figures from the International Maritime Organization show 121 confirmed attacks on merchant vessels across the region since hostilities began in late February, including 34 between September 28 and October 27. articles.title: Hengli leaps from fifth to first in global shipbuilding rankings
articles.summary: Hengli Heavy Industry has captured almost a quarter of global newbuilding business this year, an extraordinary achievement for a Chinese shipyard that was brought back from the dead just four years ago. articles.body: Greater China Shipyards Hengli leaps from fifth to first in global shipbuilding rankings Sam Chambers October 30, 2026 0 300 2 minutes read Hengli Hengli Hengli Heavy Industry has captured almost a quarter of global newbuilding business this year, an extraordinary achievement for a Chinese shipyard that was brought back from the dead just four years ago. New figures from shipbroker Banchero Costa show the Dalian-based yard secured orders for 276 ships between January and September, representing 23.4% of all compensated gross tonnage (cgt) contracted across seven major merchant shipping sectors. That compares with a 9.4% market share in 2025. The numbers are remarkable. Hengli secured orders for 117 containerships, 100 crude tankers and 39 bulk carriers during the first nine months, making it by far the world’s busiest individual shipyard for new contracts. Its outstanding orderbook has swollen to 485 ships, representing 11.2% of the global orderbook by cgt across the seven sectors, more than any other individual yard. They took the world by storm A year ago, Hengli ranked fifth globally with a 4.8% share. The gap to its nearest rivals is enormous. Hudong-Zhonghua secured 7.1% of global contracting by cgt over the same period, followed by South Korea’s HD Hyundai Heavy Industries with 6.9%. The industrial transformation has been just as spectacular as the order intake. Hengli, part of Chen Jianhua’s sprawling industrial empire, acquired the failed STX Dalian shipyard in 2022, delivering just four ships in 2024 and 17 last year. This year it has already delivered 62 ships in nine months. Banchero costa’s latest schedule shows 99 ships due for delivery next year and an astonishing 199 in 2028. On a cgt basis, Hengli alone is scheduled to account for 12.6% of all global deliveries in the seven sectors in 2028. Splash reported earlier this year that Hengli had embarked on a RMB13.5bn ($1.9bn) expansion programme, including the installation of some of the world’s largest gantry cranes, with two 2,000-tonne units spanning 256 m. The group is also investing heavily in manufacturing its own marine engines and other key equipment. Hengli’s extraordinary rise also attracted praise at this week’s Maritime CEO Forum in Monaco. Speaking during the Tanker Market Outlook session, Lars-Christian Svensen, who heads Bruton, Himalaya Shipping and OMC Tankers, highlighted the remarkable advances made by China’s newest shipbuilding giant. “They took the world by storm,” Svensen said, adding that what had been delivered so far had been “excellent”. The industrial expansion is also delivering enormous financial returns. Songfa, Hengli’s Shanghai-listed parent, reported yesterday that attributable net profit had reached RMB6.67bn ($994m) in the first nine months of 2026, up nearly 425% year-on-year. Third-quarter profit alone reached RMB3.06bn, exceeding the company’s entire 2025 earnings. There are, however, growing questions over whether the world’s shipyards can deliver everything they have sold. Banchero Costa calculates that 32.8% of all newbuilding contracting by cgt this year has gone to new or revived shipyards, the vast majority in China, with Hengli accounting for most of that business. The broker notes that Hengli’s scheduled 2028 output, measured in cgt, is approximately three and a half times its annualised production rate during the first nine months of this year. The wider Chinese shipbuilding industry faces a similar challenge, with yards scheduled to deliver 89.1m dwt of bulk carriers and tankers in 2028, compared with their previous annual record of 62.6m dwt in 2011. Banchero Costa expects some of the industry’s scheduled 2027 and 2028 deliveries to slip into later years. articles.body: The Port Authority of New York and New Jersey has announced that PATH Director and General Manager Clarelle DeGraffe will retire at the end of 2026 after more than 37 years with the agency, the last seven leading the PATH rail transit system. James Sincaglia, a long-time NJ Transit executive, has been appointed as her successor, joined by Matthew Reddell, formerly of Bay Area Rapid Transit in northern California, as deputy director for infrastructure maintenance and rolling stock delivery. Both join Zandra Ford, appointed deputy director for operations in June 2026, completing PATH’s new senior leadership team. DeGraffe will assist in the leadership transition until her retirement. DeGraffe’s tenure as PATH director from March 2019 was marked by transformative achievements. She oversaw the PATH Improvement Plan in 2019 and the PATH Forward programme concluded in March 2026, directed the US$ 2 billion reconstruction of PATH stations, tunnels and equipment devastated by Superstorm Sandy, led the system through the coronavirus pandemic, implemented the tap-to-pay TAPP fare system, oversaw major infrastructure works at Hoboken station and enabled the Every Line Every Day service expansion in spring 2025. Under her leadership in 2022, PATH received the American Public Transportation Association’s Outstanding Public Transportation System Achievement Award for railroads with more than 20 million annual riders. Port Authority Chairman Kevin O’Toole credited DeGraffe for her leadership and mentorship of female staff throughout the agency, noting that PATH has emerged from multiple challenges as a stronger and improved system. DeGraffe described the past seven years as the highlight of her Port Authority career, expressing confidence that the railroad’s leadership is in capable hands as she departs.

articles.title: Gulf Oil Producers Build Tanker Fleet as Security Risks Mount Around Hormuz
articles.summary: Gulf oil producers are assembling a fleet of nearly 230 tankers to maintain crude exports through the Strait of Hormuz despite heightened security risks and reluctance among independent shipowners to operate in the region, according to a weekly…
articles.body: Gulf Oil Producers Build Tanker Fleet as Security Risks Mount Around Hormuz Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 29, 2026 Three tankers carrying russian diesel to the U.S. © Windward Gulf oil producers are assembling a fleet of nearly 230 tankers to maintain crude exports through the Strait of Hormuz despite heightened security risks and reluctance among independent shipowners to operate in the region, according to a weekly intelligence report from Windward Maritime dated October 29. The report identifies five maritime developments, including changes to Gulf oil transportation, an oil spill threatening infrastructure in the United Arab Emirates, suspicious movements near subsea communications cables, continued Russian oil trading under sanctions pressure and shipping activity through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Gulf states expand their tanker capacity Windward describes the emergence of what it calls the “Arab Dark Fleet,” comprising tankers owned, managed, chartered or controlled by Gulf national oil companies and their trading and shipping affiliates. The fleet allows regional producers to move oil despite elevated freight costs and reduced availability of vessels willing to load at terminals in Iraq, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain, Oman and the UAE. About 80% of the fleet consists of very large crude carriers (VLCCs). Many operate with their automatic identification systems (AIS) switched off, which Windward says reflects safety and security concerns. The vessels transport crude from terminals west of Hormuz to ship-to-ship transfer hubs off the UAE and Oman, where cargoes are transferred to other tankers for onward delivery. Preliminary Vortexa figures cited by Windward indicate that crude exports, excluding Iranian shipments, from terminals west of Hormuz reached a pace of approximately 11 million barrels per day in October. That compares with 1.56 million barrels per day in May and prewar volumes of 14.5 million barrels per day. The fleet expansion has tied up an estimated 15% to 20% of the global VLCC fleet at any given time, illustrating the scale of the logistical response. Oil spill threatens UAE coastline and desalination infrastructure An oil leak from a tanker anchored approximately 25 kilometers north of Umm Al Quwain reached UAE beaches on October 22, following a forecast issued by Windward two days earlier. Authorities confirmed oil along the coast and closed beaches in Umm Al Quwain and Sharjah on October 23. Ras Al Khaimah closed all its beaches the following day after satellite imagery showed oil along the Al Hamra shoreline. Windward tracked the slick northeast along the coast toward the NAQA’A desalination plant, the largest such facility in the northern emirates. The oil came close enough to the plant’s seawater intake to pose a potential operational threat. As of the report, no desalination plant had reported a shutdown. A service vessel was observed alongside the tanker, although its precise role in containing the leak or offloading cargo remained unclear. Iranian vessels raise concerns over subsea cables Between October 14 and 28, three U.S.-sanctioned tankers and an Iranian fishing-support vessel made unusual movements near undersea communications cable routes in the Gulf of Oman and off Iran’s Makran coast, according to Windward. The vessels slowed, circled, reversed course or switched off AIS near several cable corridors. One tanker went dark for 86 hours near the 2Africa and Bay of Bengal Gateway routes before reappearing about nine nautical miles from its last reported position. Another turned back toward Oman after slowing near the 2Africa corridor. The activity coincided with statements by Iranian security and military officials threatening regional undersea cables if hostilities resumed. Windward assesses that the vessel movements could indicate cable mapping or preparations for interference, but AIS data alone cannot establish whether the ships conducted surveillance or deployed equipment. Russian oil movements continue despite sanctions Windward also identified a Russia-flagged Aframax tanker discharging approximately 700,000 barrels of Russian ESPO crude at a terminal in Dongying, China, on October 27. The tanker had switched off its AIS signal between October 24 and 28, obscuring its port call. The vessel is sanctioned by the United States, United Kingdom and European Union. Separately, three tankers carrying Russian diesel were reported heading toward the United States under a temporary U.S. sanctions waiver issued on October 9. Windward noted potential compliance challenges involving two of the vessels, which are themselves subject to sanctions. Bab el-Mandeb traffic remains steady Despite continued Houthi attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure and fighting in Yemen, vessel traffic through Bab el-Mandeb remained broadly stable. Windward recorded an average of 39 daily transits over the three-day period ending October 26, compared with approximately 35 per day since August. Saudi-affiliated vessels were notably scarce, accounting for just 13 of roughly 2,500 crossings tracked between July 20 and October 22. Windward expects these operators to continue avoiding the strait, while other shipowners maintain current transit patterns. Together, the developments highlight the operational adjustments, infrastructure vulnerabilities and sanctions-related complications confronting commercial shipping across the Middle East and beyond.

John Garamendi speaks outside the U.S. Capitol during a press conference with lawmakers, labor leaders and maritime industry representatives urging passage of the SHIPS for America Act, legislation aimed at revitalizing U.S. shipbuilding and the maritime industrial base. A bipartisan group of 119 lawmakers is urging congressional leaders to preserve and expand provisions of the SHIPS for America Act in the final fiscal year 2027 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), warning that rebuilding the U.S. maritime industry is essential to national and economic security. In an October 29 letter to House and Senate leadership, the lawmakers called for retaining shipbuilding provisions already approved by the House while considering additional measures from the broader legislation that were left out. The letter was led by Representatives Trent Kelly (R-MS) and John Garamendi (D-CA), along with Senators Todd Young (R-IN) and Mark Kelly (D-AZ), the bipartisan sponsors of the SHIPS for America Act. “As negotiations proceed on the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) for Fiscal Year 2027, we write to share our strong support for the inclusion of the bipartisan, bicameral Shipbuilding and Harbor Infrastructure for Prosperity and Security Act of 2025,” the lawmakers wrote. The push comes as Congress works to finalize the annual defense policy bill, which has emerged as a potential vehicle for advancing long-sought reforms to the U.S. commercial maritime industry. What’s in the SHIPS for America Act? Key Provisions to Restore U.S. Maritime Power The House-passed NDAA, H.R. 8800, includes elements of the SHIPS for America Act under Title XXXVI. According to the letter, those provisions were agreed to unanimously in the House. But the lawmakers argue that the measures represent only a starting point. “The inclusion of these provisions is a necessary start for revitalizing the U.S. maritime industry,” they wrote, adding that Congress should give further consideration to provisions omitted from the House-passed bill. The SHIPS for America Act is a sweeping proposal aimed at reversing decades of decline in American commercial shipbuilding and shipping. It seeks to establish long-term federal maritime policy and oversight, improve the competitiveness of U.S.-flagged vessels in international commerce, rebuild domestic shipyards, and expand recruitment, training, and retention of American mariners and shipyard workers. The lawmakers pointed to the enormous gap between U.S. shipbuilding capacity and that of its Asian competitors. China, South Korea, and Japan collectively account for more than 90% of global shipbuilding by tonnage, while the United States builds less than 1%, according to figures cited in the letter. The lawmakers also noted that fewer than 100 U.S.-flagged vessels participate in international commerce, compared with an estimated Chinese fleet of more than 5,500 ships. That imbalance, they argued, poses risks that extend well beyond commercial competition. “Especially should the United States enter a prolonged conflict, a robust Merchant Marine, outfitted with U.S. shipping vessels manned by American mariners, would be critical for addressing any potential logistical challenges associated with the transportation of supplies,” the letter states. The legislation has attracted support from maritime unions, commercial carriers, shipbuilding interests, and industry associations. The lawmakers also pointed to the Trump administration’s stated commitment to restoring U.S. maritime dominance. The latest letter demonstrates the breadth of congressional support for the initiative, with signatories spanning both parties and both chambers. Among those signing were Senators Susan Collins, Elizabeth Warren, Richard Blumenthal, Amy Klobuchar, Katie Britt, and John Fetterman, along with Representatives Joe Courtney, Rob Wittman, Salud Carbajal, and John Moolenaar, chairman of the House Select Committee on China. The lawmakers are now pressing congressional leadership to preserve those provisions and go further before the defense bill reaches the president’s desk. “Now, we ask that these provisions be retained and strengthened in the final National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027,” the letter concludes.
