articles.title: IMCA Launches 2030 Strategy to Guide Offshore Construction Industry
articles.summary: The International Marine Contractors Association (IMCA) has launched IMCA 2030, a four-year strategy designed to ensure the association remains relevant, authoritative, and valuable to members as the offshore construction industry navigates…
articles.body: IMCA Launches 2030 Strategy to Guide Offshore Construction Industry Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 29, 2026 Iain Grainger, Chief Executive Officer of IMCA. © IMCA The International Marine Contractors Association (IMCA) has launched IMCA 2030, a four-year strategy designed to ensure the association remains relevant, authoritative, and valuable to members as the offshore construction industry navigates a period of significant change. Launched at the IMCA Global Summit in Antwerp, Belgium, the strategy responds to major industry trends including the growth of AI and automation, the energy transition, evolving regulatory requirements, and increasing competition for talent and skills. At the heart of the strategy are three strategic pillars: Advocating for technical excellence and standardization, Championing a safe, skilled, and diverse workforce, and Supporting sustainability and operational efficiency. These priorities will guide IMCA’s investment, services, and activities over the coming years. “The offshore construction industry is entering a period of profound change. New technologies, changing energy markets, and increasing regulatory demands are reshaping our sector, while competition for the next generation of skilled people continues to grow," explained Iain Grainger, CEO of IMCA. “IMCA 2030 is our response to these challenges and opportunities. It sets out a clear vision for how we will champion, protect, and support our industry and its workforce, ensuring it remains safe, sustainable, and fit for the future. The strategy reinforces our commitment to technical excellence, skills and competence, sustainability, and stronger advocacy, while ensuring we continue to deliver practical value for our members worldwide.” Under the strategy, IMCA will maintain its role as a global authority in diving, dynamic positioning, safety, and ROV operations, while building on its deep expertise in offshore survey and lifting and rigging, and supporting the industry to respond to evolving digital security threats. It will also strengthen its marine division through enhanced work on autonomy and remote operations, decarbonization, and offshore wind, alongside continued investment in eCMID, IMCA’s safety management system health check for offshore vessels. A major focus of IMCA 2030 will be supporting people and skills across the industry. Planned initiatives include a campaign to raise awareness of offshore careers, additional support for early-career professionals through IMCA’s Next Generation Network, and the creation of a joined-up competence management ecosystem to support the global offshore workforce’s continuing professional development. This will be supported by new initiatives such as digital logbooks and the IMCA Skills platform, providing on-demand access to training, professional development, and competence assurance. In addition, IMCA will enhance its policy and advocacy activities. Building on its longstanding involvement with the International Maritime Organization (IMO), the Association will increase its dialogue with the European Union and with national governments and regulators. It will focus on practical, coordinated regulation that improves safety, operational efficiency, decarbonization, and industry growth, while avoiding unnecessary complexity and cost. IMCA 2030 has been informed by member engagement and feedback. It sets out plans to increase regional participation and give Members more opportunities to contribute to technical guidance and the Association's direction, in part through a new Membership Committee that reports directly to the IMCA Board. Previously announced membership changes will take effect in January 2027, introducing a simpler more transparent framework designed to strengthen member engagement, improve members’ access to IMCA’s technical resources, and better support the evolving needs of the offshore energy industry. A new Associate category will open IMCA membership to independent consultants and sole traders, alongside academic institutions and research organizations undertaking commercial research.

(Photo: Contships Management) ATHENS/SOFIA, Oct 29 (Reuters) – A Greek container ship has sunk after being hit by naval drones off Bulgaria on Wednesday, the Bulgarian government said, in the latest of a series of strikes in the western Black Sea this month that have raised concerns about the widening scope of Russia’s war in Ukraine. The Liberian-flagged CONTSHIP JET, loaded with 421 containers, was badly damaged by three sea drones as it passed through Bulgaria’s Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) – but outside its territorial waters – en route from Haifa in Israel to Constan?a in Romania. The crew of 14 Filipinos and four Ukrainians were all rescued and transferred safely to the Bulgarian port of Varna, Contships Management said. Video footage verified by Reuters showed a sea drone driving alongside the vessel before turning towards its hull. In a separate video, an explosion was seen, causing the ship to eventually list. It was not immediately clear who had carried out the attack, which added to growing concerns about the impact of Russia’s war in Ukraine on commercial shipping in the area. Ambrey, a global maritime risk management firm, has analyzed footage, reportedly filmed on a handheld device by a crew member on board, showing a matte black, 5-6 meter-long unmanned surface vehicle (USV) approaching the vessel at high speed. The USV was likely a variant of a Russian drone, said Tomas Alexa, a senior analyst at Ambrey Analytics, adding that its maneuvers indicated it was controlled remotely. “Ambrey assessed that the USV was likely a variant of, or derived from, the Russian Murena-300S design,” he told Reuters. At least six ships have been attacked by drones off Bulgaria this month, and about two dozen seafarers are feared dead, according to government statements. While it is not clear who has carried out the attacks, Bulgaria’s Prime Minister, Rumen Radev, has said that some of them appear to benefit Russia. Moscow has denied involvement in recent attacks and did not immediately comment on Wednesday’s incident. Andriy Ryzhenko, a former senior Ukrainian navy officer, said the drone visible in the video does not look similar to any model of Ukrainian naval drone that he is aware of. Bulgaria, a member of the European Union and NATO, has sought assistance to bolster security off its Black Sea coast. Bulgarian naval commander Kiril Mihaylov told national television authorities had been alerted to a possible drone attack by a French patrol aircraft, but had been unable to prevent it. The government said that initial inspections on Thursday had found no visible traces of pollution from the ship, whose cargo included lithium-ion batteries, corrosive liquids and acids and industrial components. (Image: Wallenius Wilhelmsen) Wallenius Wilhelmsen is expanding its fleet renewal program with an order for four new dual-fuel car carriers and options for eight more, potentially adding 12 vessels in a deal valued at approximately $1.5 billion. The Norwegian shipping and logistics group announced Wednesday that it has reached an agreement with China’s Jinling Shipyard (Jiangsu) for the construction of four 9,900-car-equivalent-unit (CEU) pure car and truck carriers (PCTCs), with deliveries beginning in mid-2030. The agreement includes options for four additional vessels in 2031 and another four in 2032. If all options are exercised, total capital expenditure is expected to reach approximately $1.5 billion. The ships will be equipped with dual-fuel LNG engines and built to Wallenius Wilhelmsen’s Shaper Class design , which features hoistable decks, heavy-duty ramps and flexible cargo spaces capable of accommodating passenger vehicles, trucks and other rolling equipment. The latest order expands the company’s fleet renewal program to 26 vessels, including options, extending a newbuilding campaign launched in 2023 that Wallenius Wilhelmsen describes as the largest in its history. “We continue to see attractive opportunities in the segments we serve and want to ensure we have the capacity, flexibility and efficiency needed to support our customers well into the next decades,” said Xavier Leroi, chief operating officer of shipping services at Wallenius Wilhelmsen. “Expanding our newbuilding program with deliveries from 2030 reflects our confidence in the long-term fundamentals of the market,” he added. The newbuilding agreement follows a private placement completed earlier this month as the company continues investing in its long-term fleet requirements. Wallenius Wilhelmsen has already begun taking delivery of vessels under its existing Shaper Class program, with the new ships intended to modernize its fleet while providing additional capacity across its global shipping network. The company said the vessels’ flexible cargo configurations will allow it to respond to changing customer demand across the automotive and high-and-heavy equipment markets. The investment also reinforces the company’s shift toward alternative-fuel-capable vessels. LNG dual-fuel propulsion offers a pathway to reducing certain emissions compared with conventional marine fuels, although its overall climate benefits depend in part on methane emissions and fuel sourcing. Headquartered in Oslo, Wallenius Wilhelmsen operates approximately 130 vessels across 15 trade routes serving six continents. Its broader logistics network includes vehicle processing centers, inland distribution operations and marine terminals. The company said the expanded newbuilding program will help maintain capacity and operational flexibility as it prepares for shipping demand into the next decade. articles.title: QatarEnergy Continues LNG Buying Spree to Hedge Future Hormuz Disruptions
articles.summary: QatarEnergy is buying long-term supplies of liquefied natural gas from the US and other producers as part of a trading strategy designed to generate revenue if exports through the Strait of Hormuz are disrupted in the future, CEO Saad Sherida Al-Kaabi told Reuters on Thursday.

Join the leading maritime news network Stock Image: Shutterstock/Oleksandr Kalinichenko DOHA, Oct 29 (Reuters) – QatarEnergy is buying long-term supplies of liquefied natural gas from the US and other producers as part of a trading strategy designed to generate revenue if exports through the Strait of Hormuz are disrupted in the future, CEO Saad Sherida Al-Kaabi told Reuters on Thursday. “In a scenario where you have a closure of the strait, which is the true contingency that we’re looking to have, you’d immediately see a spike in gas price and you’ll be able to generate revenue for QatarEnergy that otherwise wouldn’t be generated,” Kaabi, who is also the minister of state for energy affairs, said of the plan. Kaabi’s remarks reveal for the first time how Qatar, one of the world’s largest LNG producers, plans to offset lost income from the Iran war and protect revenue against future disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz. The company signed a 20-year agreement on Thursday to buy 3 million metric tons per year (mtpa) from Woodside’s US facilities. Last week it signed two agreements with Cheniere Energy for up to 4 mtpa through 2054 from its Sabine Pass and Corpus Christi plants. Together, the deals amount to 7 mtpa in the past two weeks. “There’s more to come,” Kaabi said. Cheniere deliveries are not expected to begin until 2031. TRADING EDGE Kaabi, appointed CEO of the state energy giant in 2014, said the strategy was his idea and took shape about three months ago after QatarEnergy studied and ruled out pipeline options. “As we have seen, pipelines and pump stations or compression stations can be also targets.” The strategy builds on QatarEnergy’s LNG expertise, trading operation and shipping fleet. It requires no capital spending and is far cheaper than building pipelines or extra LNG trains, he said. “In normal circumstances you’d make a reasonable return and in critical circumstances — however that comes out and how long it is — you have actual proof today of what you could make.” QatarEnergy halted LNG production in early March after several days of Iranian missile attacks on Qatar. It declared force majeure to affected buyers on March 4. Qatar accounts for around a fifth of global LNG exports, all of which pass through Hormuz. The company has extended force majeure until the end of 2026. Kaabi said being unable to ship volumes had taken a heavy toll on revenue. QatarEnergy believes it can leverage its fleet of about 200 LNG tankers, the world’s largest, as well as QatarEnergy Trading, which Kaabi said will soon become the world’s largest gas trading platform. “When you have the arbitrage capability that we have, the volume, number of ships, all the capabilities that we have, that’s why you can do it,” Kaabi said. The hedge targets a market transformed after Iran responded to a war launched by the US and Israel on February 28 by effectively closing the Strait of Hormuz, a vital chokepoint through which a fifth of the world’s oil and LNG shipments pass. QatarEnergy can profit from the gap between lower US gas prices and higher European prices, Kaabi said. “You can imagine the arbitrage you can make, and that would make up some of the loss.” MORE DEALS TO COME Kaabi said he expects QatarEnergy to sign more 20- to 25-year supply agreements with US and other producers this year. The company’s target is “much higher” than 7 mtpa, though Kaabi declined to give a figure. He said QatarEnergy was in talks with “everybody,” including Venture Global, and would buy from whichever supplier offered the best commercial terms. Reuters reported last week that Venture Global is in advanced talks to supply 3 mtpa. Kaabi said QatarEnergy cannot offer US volumes to long-term customers as a backup to Hormuz disruptions because long-term customer contracts are point-to-point — requiring deliveries from specific export terminals to specific destinations. He added that customers had been understanding of the disruption. Iranian missile strikes on QatarEnergy’s main Ras Laffan gas processing facility in March damaged two of its 14 LNG trains, affecting combined capacity of 12.8 mtpa and knocking out about 17% of Qatar’s export capacity. QatarEnergy said in March the damage would cost about $20 billion a year in lost revenue. Kaabi said on Thursday that repairs to the two trains would take about three years. The Pearl gas-to-liquids plant, a joint venture between QatarEnergy and Shell that was also damaged in the attack, should return to service by the first quarter of 2027, he said. He said Qatar could restart full LNG production within a week of a peace deal, provided ships were available. Output would be limited to about 83% of pre-war levels until the damaged trains return. Kaabi said no announced project had been canceled. Ras Laffan has capacity of 77 mtpa, and Qatar’s plan to expand LNG output to 142 mtpa remains unchanged, with all contracts awarded, he said. North Field East, South and West are all proceeding. The first North Field train is expected to start up in the first quarter of next year, although production would require a US-Iran peace deal to be in place. Kaabi said he had met Iran’s acting petroleum minister twice in recent weeks to explore oil and gas cooperation once the war ends. (Reporting by Andrew Mills in Doha and Maha El Dahan in Dubai. articles.summary: Nine maritime labor organizations say the Trump administration’s prolonged Jones Act waiver raises serious questions about compliance with federal law, including reporting requirements, immigration restrictions and the use of foreign...

Photo by Andy Randy Shutterstock Nine maritime labor organizations say the Trump administration’s prolonged Jones Act waiver raises serious questions about compliance with federal law, including reporting requirements, immigration restrictions and the use of foreign vessels in domestic commerce. Nine U.S. maritime labor organizations are raising fresh concerns over the Trump administration’s ongoing Jones Act waiver, warning that foreign-flagged vessels may be conducting domestic voyages without meeting federal reporting requirements and other legal safeguards intended to protect American mariners and national security. In an October 27 letter to House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee Ranking Member Rick Larsen (D-Wash.) and Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation Subcommittee Ranking Member Salud Carbajal (D-Calif.), the unions questioned whether the waiver complies with restrictions enacted under the Fiscal Year 2023 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA). The letter comes as the administration’s Jones Act waiver, first issued March 17 amid disruptions caused by the war with Iran, approaches its November 15 expiration following two extensions. The waiver allows certain foreign-flagged vessels to transport cargo between U.S. ports, temporarily setting aside the Jones Act’s requirement that domestic waterborne cargo move aboard U.S.-built, U.S.-owned and U.S.-crewed vessels. At issue is whether the waiver meets the NDAA’s requirement that such exemptions be granted only when “necessary in the interest of national defense to address an immediate adverse effect on military operations.” The unions argue that the extent of foreign-vessel activity under the waiver is difficult to reconcile with that standard. “The Administration, meanwhile, has provided Congress and the public with little of the required information regarding the need for the waivers and the availability of U.S. vessels as required by law,” the organizations wrote. They also allege that some waiver recipients have submitted inadequate documentation, missed mandatory reporting deadlines or failed to report their voyages altogether. Under federal requirements, vessel operators must submit post-voyage reports to the Maritime Administration within 10 days, including details about the vessel, cargo, ports visited and why the voyage served national defense interests. According to the unions, many operators have provided generic explanations or simply responded “not applicable” when asked to explain the national defense justification for their movements. Foreign Crews Raise Additional Legal Questions The labor organizations also raised concerns about the use of foreign mariners aboard vessels operating in U.S. domestic commerce, including potential violations of immigration, employment and tax laws. The letter specifically questions whether foreign crewmembers holding D-1 visas are legally permitted to work aboard vessels transporting cargo between U.S. ports. “Immigration law, for example, prohibits foreign crewmembers holding a D-1 visa from engaging in domestic commerce, yet many waiver operations appear to employ precisely such D-1 visa mariners,” the unions wrote. The organizations also pointed to recent Internal Revenue Service guidance raising questions about U.S. tax obligations for foreign vessel operators and mariners participating in domestic transportation. They argue that allowing foreign crews to perform domestic shipping work without meeting comparable legal, licensing and security requirements puts American mariners at a competitive disadvantage. The letter further raises national security concerns, citing reported use of the waiver by Chinese state-owned shipping company COSCO and a separate instance involving Russian mariners. “These concerns are especially troubling because the Jones Act waiver authority was intended to strengthen national security,” the organizations wrote. “Instead, the program appears to have enabled hundreds of domestic voyages by foreign vessels crewed by foreign mariners operating under exemptions from laws that Congress never intended to set aside.” The unions cite media reports alleging espionage activity involving COSCO vessels near U.S. coastlines, but the letter does not establish that any vessel operating under the waiver engaged in espionage. Oversight Pressure Builds The latest letter adds to mounting congressional scrutiny of the waiver, including questions raised by Carbajal earlier this month over foreign-vessel reporting and compliance with federal law. As gCaptain reported on October 19, Carbajal asked Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin to explain how the department is enforcing immigration, tax and maritime requirements aboard foreign vessels operating under the waiver. That inquiry followed gCaptain’s September reporting identifying evidence of at least 14 previously unreported domestic tanker voyages and a possible 15th, expanding on a Bloomberg Government investigation that found foreign vessels had transported more than $40 million in petroleum products without appearing in MARAD’s public waiver records. A gCaptain review of MARAD data published September 16 counted 255 completed movements under the original waiver and its first extension. The additional voyages suggested the official tally was incomplete. MARAD previously told Bloomberg Government that it lacks legal authority to compel operators to submit required reports. Jones Act enforcement falls to U.S. Customs and Border Protection. The administration has since tightened its waiver procedures. Under rules introduced with the August 17 extension, operators must submit vessel availability requests before conducting a voyage, allowing MARAD to assess whether a qualified U.S.-flag vessel is available. The Department of War then determines whether the movement qualifies under the waiver. Whether those changes have addressed the broader compliance concerns remains an open question. Carbajal has requested a response from DHS by October 31. The October 27 letter was signed by leaders of nine maritime labor organizations, including the Seafarers International Union, American Maritime Officers, Marine Engineers’ Beneficial Association, Masters, Mates and Pilots, Sailors’ Union of the Pacific, American Radio Association, Marine Firemen’s Union, AFL-CIO Maritime Trades Department and AFL-CIO Transportation Trades Department. “American mariners stand ready to support the nation’s energy, transportation, and national security needs,” the unions wrote. “We ask only for a faithful enforcement of the laws enacted by Congress.” Sign up for gCaptain’s newsletter and never miss an update Essential maritime and offshore news, insights, and updates delivered daily straight to your inbox Dive into a sea of curated content with our weekly ‘Dispatch’ email. Join the leading maritime news network Photo: Royal Dutch Shell LONDON, Oct 29 (Reuters) – Shell and TotalEnergies reported on Thursday sharply higher third-quarter profits and raised share buybacks, as war-driven energy prices and record refining margins helped both beat expectations. Shell raised its quarterly buyback to $5 billion from $3 billion, the second-largest buyback on record, while Total reiterated plans to buy back $2.5 billion of shares in the fourth quarter and said it would buy back another $2.5 billion in the first quarter of 2027. The shareholder distributions offer an insight into how oil majors plan to spend the profits generated by the US-Israeli war with Iran, which is in its ninth month and has disrupted global energy supplies. Energy prices have driven inflation for customers globally and increased input costs for industry. Reflecting its higher payout, shares in Shell gained 3.2% in early trade on Thursday, while Total’s rose 1.8%, compared with a broader index of European energy companies rising 1.9%. BP, Chevron and ExxonMobil report results on Friday. Also on Thursday, Austria’s OMV reported its highest quarterly operating profit since 2022. Refining margins nearly quadrupled for both Shell and Total compared with a year ago. They reached $42 a barrel and $33.2 per barrel, respectively, helping to boost earnings to the highest since 2022, when Shell delivered a record $6 billion buyback program. Shell posted third-quarter net profit of $10.81 billion, above analysts’ average estimate of $10.33 billion and almost double the $5.43 billion it earned a year earlier. TotalEnergies reported adjusted net income of $9.1 billion for the July to September quarter, more than double the $4.0 billion a year earlier and above an expected $8.3 billion. Total’s refining and chemicals division posted record net income of $3.6 billion, more than five times the level of a year ago and double the previous quarter. CEO Patrick Pouyanné said a nearly 10% increase in refining throughput, along with strong oil trading, had captured historically high refining margins in Europe and worldwide. Total’s income in its LNG unit rose to $1.9 billion on average gas prices that were up 20% compared to the last quarter and strong LNG and gas trading. The company’s gearing fell to 9.1% at end-September from 13.1% at the end of the prior quarter, below its target of under 10% by the end of 2026. Jefferies called Total’s results “solid, not standout,” as hydrocarbon production reached 2.5 million barrels of oil equivalent per day, missing Total’s consensus by 4%, the broker said. Total also took a $1.9 billion impairment mainly tied to offshore wind and a South Korean petrochemical stake. Since December 30, 2022, Shell has delivered a 120% total shareholder return, including reinvested dividends, ahead of BP’s 78%, TotalEnergies’ TTEF.PA 84%, ExxonMobil’s 89% and Chevron’s 51%, according to Shell data. Shell beat expectations across all its segments. Its cash flow from operations, excluding working capital, rose to $21.7 billion from $12.24 billion a year earlier and beat expectations of $18.18 billion. RBC analyst Biraj Borkhataria said even with a roughly $5 billion buyback next quarter, Shell will likely miss its 40% to 50% payout ratio guidance for the year, a shortfall he attributed to abnormal macro conditions. Shell’s oil and gas output fell 17% in the first nine months of 2026 from a year earlier, mainly because war in the Middle East reduced volumes from Qatar. LNG liquefaction volumes rose 12%, driven by the ramp-up at LNG Canada and partly offset by the Qatari disruption. Shell halted production at its Pearl gas-to-liquids plant in Qatar in March after an attack on Ras Laffan Industrial City damaged one of its two trains. It has has restarted the plant but at reduced output and says repairs could take about a year. Shell recorded $5.4 billion in non-cash increases to shipping leases, which count toward net debt. Shell booked an impairment of around $2 billion across its European biogas business, which includes assets from its 2023 $2 billion acquisition of Denmark-based Nature Energy, due to lowered expectations of growth in the market. Shell lowered its capital expenditure guidance for 2026 to $23 billion to $25 billion from $24 billion to $26 billion. Image courtesy Equinor Delays involving U.S.-built support vessels have pushed back turbine installation at Equinor’s Empire Wind offshore wind project off New York, with first power now expected in the first half of 2027. Norwegian energy giant Equinor said Thursday that the 810-megawatt project is approximately 80% complete, but construction delays affecting specialized vessels needed to install its 54 wind turbines have pushed the schedule back several months. The update came as Equinor reported its third-quarter 2026 financial results. “Most of the remaining project scope relates to offshore turbine installation, which is expected to start next year,” Equinor Chief Financial Officer Torgrim Reitan told investors. “This is a bit later than planned.” The delay underscores the challenges of building out the U.S. offshore wind industry, particularly its reliance on specialized vessels and domestic shipbuilding capacity to meet requirements under the Jones Act. Empire Wind is using a turbine installation system developed by Maersk Offshore Wind, centered on the Singapore-built installation vessel Maersk Viridis . Because the vessel is foreign-built, it cannot transport turbine components between U.S. points under the Jones Act. Instead, the project relies on specially designed U.S.-built barges and tugs to deliver turbine components from the South Brooklyn Marine Terminal to the installation vessel offshore. The barges are designed to connect directly to Maersk Viridis , allowing turbine components to be transferred for installation without the installation vessel returning to port. While Maersk Viridis arrived off Pascagoula, Mississippi, in August for testing and preparations, delays involving the U.S.-built support vessels have pushed back the turbine installation campaign. Equinor said all 54 turbine foundations have been completed, along with the offshore substation and cable work. The project is located approximately 14 miles south of Long Island and is expected to generate enough electricity to power roughly 500,000 New York homes once operational. Despite the schedule setback, Equinor said it does not expect any change to the project’s total capital expenditure, although some spending will shift from 2026 into 2027. The company has previously estimated the project’s total investment, including redevelopment of the South Brooklyn Marine Terminal, at approximately $7.5 billion. Equinor also expects approximately $2.5 billion in U.S. investment tax credits, with roughly $2 billion expected to be recognized in 2027 and the remaining $500 million in 2028. The company said the revised construction schedule is not expected to affect the timing of those tax credits. The latest delay follows a turbulent period for Empire Wind, which has faced repeated attempts by the Trump administration to halt construction. The administration first ordered work stopped in April 2025, citing concerns over the project’s federal permitting process. That order was lifted the following month. A second suspension followed in December 2025, when the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management ordered construction halted on Empire Wind and four other offshore wind projects over national security concerns. Equinor challenged the suspension in federal court and secured preliminary relief allowing construction to continue. In its third-quarter financial statements, Equinor said the court dismissed the case on September 30, 2026, after the suspension order expired. The company said the dismissal eliminated the risk that a $2.7 billion project loan could become repayable within 12 months as a result of the order. Empire Wind remains one of the largest offshore wind projects under construction in the United States, with its latest setback highlighting the growing importance of domestic vessel construction to the industry’s ability to deliver projects on schedule. Join the leading maritime news network Photo credit: EB Adventure/Shutterstock (Bloomberg) — Cosco Shipping Holdings Co. earnings jumped the most in two years as persistent geopolitical disruptions rerouted trade routes, tying up more of its vessels for longer while container rates surged. Third-quarter net income rose 81% to 17.2 billion yuan ($2.6 billion), with transpacific sailings the biggest growth driver, according to a Thursday filing. Cosco’s strong showing foreshadows a bumper season for some of its global peers. Earnings estimates for Europe’s A.P. Moller-Maersk A/S and Hapag-Lloyd AG have ticked up since July. Japan’s Nippon Yusen KK’s raised outlook surpassed analyst expectations earlier on Thursday, while Taiwan’s Evergreen Marine Corp. is set for its most profitable quarter since 2024 when it reports next month. Global supply chains remained stretched throughout the quarter as vessels continue to route sailings between Asia and Europe around Africa’s Cape of Good Hope to avoid the Middle East. That’s pushed spot rates for a 40-foot container near two-year highs, a level that held for most of the quarter, according to Drewry World Container Index data. Container spot rates are likely to stay where they are, with transpacific spot rates remaining firmly anchored near post-pandemic highs amid resilient US trade flows, said Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Lindsay Chen. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P.
